title: Distributed Tracing
seoTitle: Design a Distributed Tracing System Like Jaeger or Zipkin
description: Design distributed tracing — propagating trace context across services, collecting spans, sampling strategies, storage, and assembling traces for debugging.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is Distributed Tracing?
blocks.text: In a microservice system, one user request may touch dozens of services. Distributed tracing records each hop as a **span** and links them into a **trace**, so engineers can see exactly where time was spent and where errors occurred — like Jaeger, Zipkin or Datadog APM.

items: Services should record spans (operation, start/end time, tags, errors) for the work they do.
Spans from all services involved in one request should be linked into a single trace.
Engineers should be able to look up a trace by ID and view it as a timeline.
Engineers should be able to search traces by service, operation, duration and error status.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Negligible overhead on instrumented services (< 1% CPU, no added request latency).
Handle millions of spans per second across the fleet.
Traces queryable within ~1 minute of the request completing.
Losing some spans is acceptable; tracing must never break production traffic.
Long-term retention beyond a few weeks.

lines: - lossy is ok, never break prod
blocks.caption: Tracing Requirements

items: **Trace**: all spans sharing a trace ID.
**Span**: spanId, parentSpanId, traceId, service, operation, start, duration, tags, status.
**Trace context**: traceId + parent spanId + sampling flag, propagated between services.

blocks.text: A tracing SDK (e.g. OpenTelemetry) creates spans around incoming requests and outgoing calls, buffering finished spans in memory and exporting them asynchronously in batches to a local **agent**. Export never blocks the request; if buffers fill, spans are dropped.

When service A calls service B, it injects the trace context into request headers. B continues the trace with A's span as its parent. Every span carries the same trace ID, so the backend can reassemble the tree.
3) Look up a trace by ID

Collectors write spans to storage keyed by trace ID (e.g. Cassandra partitioned by traceId, or columnar object storage). Fetching a trace is one partition read; the UI builds the tree from parent IDs and renders a timeline.
An index stores per-trace summaries (root service, operation, duration, error flag, timestamps) for filtering; matching trace IDs are then fetched from span storage.
1) How do we keep overhead and volume manageable?

challenges.text: Millions of spans per second costs a fortune to store, and most traces are boring successes.

approach.text: Decide at the root (e.g. keep 1%) and propagate the decision in the trace context so all services agree.

challenges.text: Cheap and consistent, but rare errors and slow outliers are mostly discarded before anyone knows they're interesting.

approach.text: Services send all spans to collectors; collectors buffer spans grouped by trace ID for a short window (~10-30s), then decide: keep every trace with errors or high latency, plus a small random sample of normal ones. Route spans for the same trace to the same collector (hash on traceId).

challenges.text: Collectors need memory to buffer, and late-arriving spans may miss the decision window.

blocks.text: 2) How do we store and query spans efficiently?

Write spans to a store optimised for appends with TTL-based expiry (e.g. 7-14 days). Partition by trace ID for whole-trace reads. Maintain a separate summary index (service, operation, duration buckets, error, time) — often a columnar store — for search. Derive service dependency graphs and latency histograms with a streaming job over the span stream.

quiz.question: How do spans from different services end up in the same trace?
options: Propagating trace context (traceId, parent spanId) in request headers
quiz.explanation: Each downstream span inherits the trace ID and records its parent.

quiz.question: What is the weakness of head-based sampling?
options: The keep/drop decision happens before you know whether the trace is interesting
quiz.explanation: Rare errors and slow traces are mostly dropped.

quiz.question: Why route all spans of a trace to the same collector for tail sampling?
options: The collector needs the complete trace to decide whether to keep it
quiz.explanation: Decisions require seeing every span of the trace.

quiz.question: What should the SDK do if its export buffer fills up?
quiz.explanation: Tracing must never degrade production traffic.
